title: Choking, adult and child
summary: Adult or child over 1 year who cannot cough, speak or breathe: 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.

steps.text: Is the person a baby under 1 year old?
steps.detail:
Babies under about 1 year are treated differently: back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts. Use the Choking, infant protocol.

This protocol is for adults and for children from about 1 year old.

ask.q: Is it a baby under 1 year old?

steps.detail: Go back to the Emergency screen or search for Choking, infant. Abdominal thrusts are not used on babies because they can injure the organs in the belly.

steps.text: Ask: "Are you choking?" Can they cough forcefully, speak, or cry?
steps.detail:
Signs of a severe blockage: a weak cough or no cough, not able to cough, cry or speak, or a panicked, confused or surprised look.

If they can cough, cry or speak, air is still moving. Encourage them to keep coughing and watch them closely instead of hitting or squeezing.

ask.q: Can they cough forcefully, speak or cry?

steps.text: Encourage them to keep coughing. Stay with them and watch closely.
steps.detail:
Do not slap their back or do thrusts while they can cough strongly.

Watch for the cough becoming weak or silent, breathing getting harder, or the person no longer able to speak. If that happens, start back blows and thrusts.

ask.q: Has the cough become weak or silent, or can they no longer speak or breathe?

steps.text: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Start helping right away.
steps.detail:
Severe choking can quickly lead to the heart stopping, so act immediately. Send someone else to get help; do not leave the person to do it yourself.

If you are alone and choking yourself (Red Cross): give yourself abdominal thrusts with your hands, the same way as for another person, or bend over and press your belly hard against a firm object such as the back of a chair. Do not use anything with a sharp edge or corner.

steps.text: Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Stop as soon as the object comes out.
steps.detail:
Stand to the side and slightly behind them. Put one arm diagonally across their chest and bend them forward at the waist so the upper body is about level with the ground.

Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand, up to 5 times, each blow separate. If the object comes out and they can cough, speak or breathe, stop.

For a small child, kneel behind them rather than stand.

The current guideline (AHA 2025) starts with back blows: in a study of 709 choking cases, back blows were linked with clearing the blockage more often and with fewer injuries than abdominal thrusts. Earlier editions started with abdominal thrusts.

ask.q: Are they in late pregnancy, or too large to reach around?

steps.text: Give 5 abdominal thrusts: from behind, fist just above the belly button, other hand over it, pull sharply in and up.
steps.detail:
Have them stand up straight. Find their belly button with two fingers. Move behind them and wrap your arms around their waist; for a child, kneel behind them. If they are in a wheelchair, give abdominal thrusts as usual; you may need to kneel behind the wheelchair, and remove the armrests if they are in the way (Red Cross).

Make a fist with your other hand and put the thumb side against the belly just above your fingers (just above the belly button). Cover the fist with your first hand.

Pull sharply inward and upward. Make each thrust forceful and separate from the last. Give up to 5.

This is the Heimlich maneuver.

ask.q: Is the object out, or are they coughing, speaking or breathing again?

steps.text: Give 5 chest thrusts instead: from behind, arms around the chest, fist on the middle of the breastbone, thrust firmly backward.
steps.detail:
When: AHA 2025 says chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy or when you cannot get your arms around the belly. Red Cross says use them for anyone obviously or known to be pregnant, or too large to wrap your arms around. For someone in a wheelchair, Red Cross says give abdominal thrusts as usual and use chest thrusts only if abdominal thrusts are difficult.

How (MedlinePlus, US National Library of Medicine): stand behind them and wrap your arms around their chest. Put the thumb side of your fist on the middle of the breastbone, level with the nipples, and cover it with your other hand. Give firm thrusts straight backward. Give up to 5, each forceful and separate.

ask.q: Is the object out, or are they coughing, speaking or breathing again?

steps.text: Not cleared? Keep repeating 5 back blows and 5 thrusts until it comes out or they collapse.
steps.detail: Keep going in cycles: 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal (or chest) thrusts, until the object comes out and they can cough, speak or breathe, or until they become unresponsive.

steps.text: They collapsed: lower them to the ground on their back and start CPR, beginning with chest compressions.
steps.detail:
Ease them down to a firm, flat surface so they do not hit their head. Start CPR straight away with compressions (use CPR, adult or CPR, child). Do not check for a pulse first.

Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth. If you can see the object, take it out. Never sweep a finger blindly in the mouth; only remove an object you can see.

If help has not been called yet, do it now. Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Cleared. Stay with them, let them rest, and watch their breathing.
steps.detail:
Keep watching their breathing and how alert they are. If breathing gets worse again, start this protocol again.

Thrusts can cause injuries. Anyone who needed thrusts, or who still has trouble breathing or pain after the object came out, should be checked by a medical professional.

steps.text: Keep encouraging coughing and stay with them until they breathe easily.
steps.detail: If at any point the cough becomes weak or silent, or they cannot speak or breathe, start this protocol again and go straight to back blows.

donts: Do not hit the back or do thrusts on someone who can cough strongly.
Do not do abdominal thrusts on a baby under 1 year; use the Choking, infant protocol.
Do not do abdominal thrusts on someone in late pregnancy or whom you cannot reach around; use chest thrusts.
Do not do blind finger sweeps in the mouth; only remove an object you can see.
Do not leave a choking person alone to go for help.
evacuate: Evacuate urgently anyone who lost consciousness or needed CPR.
Get medical evaluation for anyone who needed abdominal or chest thrusts, or who has ongoing cough, pain or trouble breathing.
